blocks.text: “Coming soon!” The words spread across the windows of closed stores, above newspapers pasted up as makeshift curtains. Opening shortly, a promise of the new. Trent Parke has made it the title of his new book, Coming Soon , and the cover itself is dressed in those stopgap papers. What remains to be seen is what is really coming, and what is leaving.

In the early 2000s, the Australian photographer took to the road with his family. Several journeys, along the east, south and west coasts. In the dust of the asphalt, a country was changing its skin without warning. Corner stores closing, seaside resorts losing their accent, globalization landing, discreet as a bulldozer. “The places we used to go to as kids on family holidays were being torn down and developed at a rapid rate,” he recalls. So he wanted to record what it all looked like “before it changed forever.”

blocks.text: To do so, one clear choice: color. No black-and-white poetry, though that is where he made his name. He needed to read every detail, “how much things cost, the flux of everything moving, the advance of technology,” and always, “the continual study of light and time.” Medium-format film, then, and primary colors taken at the source: garish signs, cheap motels, storefronts, an Australian sun that gives no quarter.

The result? An inventory without nostalgia, but not without tenderness. A bakery “open seven days,” a red car parked in front, blue sky thrown in: it looks like a postcard nobody would send. A green neon motel sign, a red light, a McDonald’s tucked into an old building, an empty street: everything is there, except the people. Further on, a white cut-out silhouette, a man in a suit holding a camera (or is it his double?), planted at the foot of an office block, palm trees all around. Further still, a dog caught mid-leap on a billboard, flung against the sky, more alive than any passerby. Irony? Of course. Parke doesn’t preach, he winks. He photographs the prices, the logos, the capital letters planted on façades, that standard vocabulary spreading everywhere and ending up speaking in place of people. Every detail becomes a piece of evidence, but played lightly, almost whistling. The red of a car body, the blue of a cloudless sky: light does the rest, brutal, joyful, a little cruel.

blocks.text: From the outback to faded seaside towns, from these fake paradises to the big city, the book moves by slippage. And it is there, in the heart of the concrete, that the image tightens. Backlit crowds, sun hammering between the towers, long shadows on the sidewalk: surrounded on all sides, and yet alone. Tough stuff. Sometimes the same street returns in variations, like a contact sheet, bus shelters, posters, silhouettes drifting in and out of the frame, as if the photographer were waiting for the setting, in the end, to give up its secret. Then night falls: a freeway, red trails, the city lighting up in the distance. Curtain.

The era is well drawn. Giant screens, outsized billboards, endless skyscrapers, everything “upsized.” The book too, and that is the least it could do: an oversized volume, with several gatefolds to unfold, like opening a road map on the hood of a car. Heavy going, the format? A bit. It took at least that much to hold the sky and the din.

blocks.text: Another, more surprising idea: the artist Jesse Feinman has taken fragments of Parke’s photographs and reworked them into new compositions. Each, they say, keeps something of the emotional charge of the original. One might see it as a way of extending the sign, the collage, the scrap of paper covering the window. Or a slightly gratuitous sidestep. Each reader can judge from the pieces themselves.

What strikes you, ultimately, is the moment chosen. Parke catches Australia in that brief window when you could still see both things at once, what it had been and what it was about to become. The span of a roll of film. Twenty years on, the country he photographed no longer exists, or almost, and the one that replaced it looks like all the others. Hence the title, a pirouette of sorts: Coming Soon , which is to say yesterday.
Coming Soon , by Trent Parke, is published by Stanley Barker and available for £85.
